newsitem.title: UK: Russian comments confuse precious metals market.
newsitem.headline: Russian comments confuse precious metals market.

text.p: Palladium and platinum prices seeswed on Thursday on apparently contradictory reports about when Russia may resume delayed exports of the rare white metals to its biggest market, Japan.
Trade sources in Japan said a Russian delegation may arrive next week to begin negotiations but officials in Moscow said they had no knowedge of such a thing.
"The market's initial preception of the news was that Russia is back in the fray,"one analyst said.
Platinum was indicated at $370.00/$371.00 per ounce up $8.00 from Wednesday and palladium was at $151.50/$152.50 after both had lost about three dollars earlier.

The issue was complicated by a statement from the first deputy prime minister and finance minister, Anatoly Chubais, that he proposed to raise more than $5 billion through the sale of precious metals and through privatisation measures.
"We need an emergency revenue programme to bring in 30 trillion roubles," Chubais told the Federation Council upper house of parliament.
"This will be through new approaches to the precious metals market, the equities market, the alcohol monopoly and highly efficient privatisation projects," he said.
Sales of gold and diamonds are traditionally a way to bring money to state coffers from precious metals.

"He (Chubais) is the first deputy prime minister so this is a high level statement that also has the involvement of the central bank. These are the levels at which the decision will be made," said Andy Smith, precious metals analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
He added "this knocks out" rumours that they are getting money from elsewhere and wondered whether the way that Chubais put metals first in his statement was "a slip or a signal."

Russia, the largest supplier of palladium and second largest exporter of platinum, has not exported either metal this year due to administrative snares and the lack of the president's signature on the essential export decree.
"If Chubais speaks, you could surmise that somebody is going to sign off on it. When the exports start depends on what is holding it up but the guess would be sooner rather than later," Smith said

Traders in Tokyo said that Russian central bank officials had told precious metals dealers in Tokyo a delegation would arrive in Japan next month to negotiate terms for the long delayed 1997 export contract to the world's largest importer of platinum group metals (PGMS).
But central bank officials in Moscow later denied this.
"The contradictory comments look like a typical wrangle between the central bank and Almaz (the export agency)," said analyst Rhona O'Connell at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co.
She added it looked like Russia was trying to appease the market. "Perhaps the central bank is being careful and doesn't want to say anything until it is cast in stone," she suggested.
Raising money by new approach to preciious metals sales was "very difficult to work out," one analyt said.

"For instance if they limit sales to get a higher price with (say) palladium at above $160, it would start to kill off some of big markets and ultimately boomerang on them. The story raises more questions than answers," the analyst said.
Another market analyst said it was relatively easy to sell gold because the market was big enough and liquid enough to absorb steady sales from a central bank

"It's not so easy with PGMs because of the tighter, more restricted nature of the market so it might be more effective for them to be more discerning, and sell only into a market which really needs the metal so that the revenue per ounce is better. It's not so easy to determine an approach."
Some industry sources said Almaz expected the decree to be signed next week and to start exporting in May. However, recent statements from the central bank suggested exports would begin in June.
